title: Full Scottish Breakfast
subtitle: Bacon, square sausage, egg, black pudding, haggis, and tattie scone
excerpt: Scotland's answer to the cooked breakfast, built around square sausage and black pudding alongside the usual bacon and egg. A proper weekend plate.
sourceNotes: Traditional Scottish cooked breakfast, a regional variation of the full cooked breakfast common across Britain. Square sausage (Lorne sausage) and tattie scones are the defining Scottish elements.

recipe.temperatureNote: Oven temperature for keeping cooked items warm while you finish the plate

glossaryTerms.definition: To spoon hot fat or cooking juices over food as it cooks, keeping it moist and helping it colour evenly.
To melt the fat slowly out of meat (especially bacon or black pudding) over moderate heat, which crisps the meat and releases flavour.

content.text: A full Scottish breakfast is built around two things you won't find on any other national version: the square-cut Lorne sausage and thick rounds of black pudding. It gives you everything the full English offers and then some. The richness makes it a weekend plate rather than a weekday one. The key to getting it right is working in the right order: the items that take longest go in first, the eggs go in last, and everything else stays warm in a low oven while you pull the plate together.
What you need

items.prepNote: square Lorne sausage slices if available, otherwise pork sausages

content.text: Fry the meats
Heat your oven to 180 °C to keep things warm as you go. Put the baking tray inside. Set the large frying pan over medium heat and add the olive oil. Lay the
sausages
in the pan and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, turning every couple of minutes until browned on all sides and cooked through. Transfer to the warm baking tray in the oven.
In the same pan, add the
back-bacon
rashers. Let them
render
for 2 to 3 minutes per side until the fat is golden and the edges just begin to crisp. Move to the oven. Add the
black-pudding
slices to the pan, they need only 2 minutes per side. They firm up and develop a dark crust without any added fat; there is enough in the pudding itself. Add to the oven.
Add the butter to the pan and cook the
mushrooms-chestnut
cut-side down for 3 minutes without moving them, then turn and cook 1 minute more. Push them to one side and add the
tomato
halves cut-side down for 3 minutes. Season both with salt and pepper and transfer to the oven.
Cook the eggs
Wipe the large pan clean with kitchen paper and set the small frying pan over medium-low heat. Add a small knob of butter. Crack the
eggs
in carefully. Cook for 2 to 3 minutes, tilting the pan and spooning the hot butter over the whites to
baste
them gently. The whites should be fully set with a still-runny yolk. If you prefer the yolk set, cover the pan with a lid for the final 30 seconds.
Bring it together

Pull everything from the oven. Arrange on two warm plates: sausage, bacon, black pudding, mushrooms, and tomato first, then slide the egg on top or alongside. If you're serving baked beans, warm them in a small pan and spoon them into a section of the plate so they don't flood everything else. Serve immediately, a full Scottish waits for no one.
Troubleshooter

Black pudding falls apart in the pan: the pan isn't hot enough before you add it, or you're moving it too soon. Let it sit undisturbed for the full 2 minutes before attempting to turn it. A good crust on one side holds the slice together.

Sausages burnt outside but raw inside: the heat is too high. Reduce to medium-low and give them a longer, gentler cook. Square sausage slices are thinner than links so they cook faster, 6 to 8 minutes is usually enough.
Where this dish lives

The full Scottish breakfast is a fixture of Scottish café culture. You'll find it in greasy-spoon diners from Dumfries to Inverness and in every B&B that takes its reputation seriously. The Lorne sausage is the defining element: a flat, square-cut beef and pork patty, quite different from the curved pork links of an English breakfast. Tattie scones are another traditional addition, thin pan-fried potato cakes that soak up the cooking juices beautifully. They're not listed here as a separate ingredient, but they're worth making or buying if you can find them. Haggis, when added, turns this into a very serious plate indeed.
